topics.topic: Audit sequence recorded and checked when entries have been erased or none exist
questions: After audit erasure removes the entry with the greatest sequence number, does the backup record and check the persistent next-sequence counter, the greatest surviving entry, or both; and what value is recorded when no audit entry survives?
What sequence value is recorded and how is the check evaluated when the audit log has never contained an entry?
What sequence value is recorded and checked when the audit log has never contained an entry?

judgement.why: This is the same empty-audit-log backup metadata and validation question already assigned to State 6.

precedent.topic: Metadata and validation semantics for an empty audit log in a backup
quotes:
It
   records, readable without its key, its instant, the release that made it,
   the last audit sequence number it holds and a digest of the key it was
   made with (never the key); its age is counted from that instant.

Second, it
   writes the backup under a temporary name and checks it: it decrypts it
   into a second temporary file, opens that for reading only, checks that it
   is the store version of its release, that the store's own integrity check
   passes and that its audit log ends at the recorded sequence number, and
   removes it; a backup that passes is renamed to its kept name, one that
   fails is deleted.
precedent.why: The empty-log representation of the sequence metadata and its encoded validation rule are field-type and backup-format contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Backup encryption, nonce, key identifier, authenticated metadata, and container format
questions: Which authenticated-encryption algorithm, nonce construction, key derivation or key encoding, key-digest algorithm and encrypted container format are required?
What cryptographic format protects the backup ciphertext and binds its public metadata against tampering?
What cryptographic construction makes a backup confidential and detects tampering, and how are its nonce, authenticated metadata and non-secret key identifier produced?

judgement.why: This repeats the previously judged question about the backup encryption envelope, authentication, nonce, key representation and metadata binding.

precedent.topic: Backup authenticated-encryption format, metadata binding, key digest, and key requirements
quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
precedent.why: The algorithm, nonce, authenticated envelope, key identifier and cryptographic-version representation are encoding and file-format contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Backup-run success and status when retention cleanup fails
questions: If a new backup is successfully kept but deletion of one expired or unreadable kept file fails, is the overall run successful or failed, what does the owner-facing newest-backup status show, and is the kept new backup retained?
What is the run's result when backup creation succeeds but one or more retention deletions fail?
Does any unreadable or undeletable kept file make the whole run failed, and what exact combination of backup creation, checking, renaming and retention-cleanup results counts as a successful run?

quotes: Third, whatever the second step did, it deletes every kept backup made more than 30 × 24 hours before, and every file under the kept prefix whose unencrypted record (rule 1) cannot be read.
It takes the files in the order of their names; a file it cannot read or delete is reported, and it goes on with the next.

A step that fails leaves no partial kept backup — at most a file under the temporary prefix, which the next run removes — and writes a diagnostic that names the failure and no value (A17); Registry keeps serving, and the next 03:00 tries again.

While the daily runs succeed, an erasure reaches the backups by the first run after the last backup holding the erased values is 30 days old — at most 31 days after the erasure — and a failed or missed run lengthens that by the days until a run succeeds.

after a run whose deletions succeeded: no backup older than 30 days and no
  backup that failed its check exists
judgement.divergence: One implementation keeps the newly created backup but marks the run failed whenever any retention deletion fails; another treats creation as successful and reports cleanup failures separately. The owner monitoring backup success and retention notices the difference.
judgement.why: The rules describe continuing after cleanup failures but do not define whether such a run succeeded or whether success is divisible between creation and retention cleanup.

topics.topic: Behavior of mapping, confirmation, and sign-out requests after finding migration closure
questions: When the migration closure exists, which of mapping display, confirmation-step display and sign-out are refused, and which continue normally after checking it?
What must each mapping, confirmation-step, and sign-out request do when it finds the migration closure?
What does a closure found by showing the mapping, showing the import confirmation step, or signing out do?

quotes: Uploads and every other request that reads or changes an uploaded file — showing the mapping or the import's confirmation step, confirming, a sign-out — take the instance's one import lock first, then their session's lock (A13), check the closure while holding them, and hold both until done.
While the closure exists, uploading and confirming an import are refused (R0-79).
judgement.divergence: One implementation refuses mapping display, confirmation-step display and sign-out when it finds the closure; another refuses only upload and confirmation while allowing the other requests to finish normally. The signed-in owner notices which pages and sign-out remain usable.
judgement.why: The text requires all these requests to check the closure but specifies the consequence only for uploading and confirming.

topics.topic: Exact configuration variable names, encodings, syntax, and value validation
questions: What are the exact environment-variable names and the accepted textual syntax and normalization rules for each location, credential, token and backup key?
What are the exact accepted REGISTRY_ variable names, encodings, and well-formedness conditions for paths, credentials, tokens, and the backup key?

What are the exact REGISTRY_ variable names and how are store paths, backup paths, credentials, tokens and the backup key decoded and validated, including what counts as a byte for the 32-byte minimum?

judgement.why: This repeats the previously judged request for the complete configuration schema, names, encodings and validation rules.

precedent.topic: Complete configuration schema, including accepted variable names and validation rules
quotes:
The configuration is the set of environment variables whose names begin
   with `REGISTRY_`, set as R0-23 says; no other variable is read or
   checked.

It holds exactly these items and no other: the store's
   location; the backup location and the backup key (A18); the owner
   credential; one service token for each service of A09 — PresuPro, Client
   Portal, Cabinet, Cabinet Kernel (R0-20, R0-23) — or, for an owner-only
   start, none of the four: Registry then serves the owner interface alone
   and refuses every service call (A18 rule 9).
precedent.why: Exact environment-variable names, value encodings, path syntax and structural validity rules are configuration-schema and encoding details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Timing and guarantees for deleting uploads when owner sessions expire
questions: Is an upload destroyed at the instant its session reaches a lifetime limit, or may its personal data remain in memory until some later request acquires the import lock; and what happens if no later holder ever arrives?
Does expiry drop the uploaded file immediately, or may its personal data remain in memory until another request takes the import lock?
Does the uploaded file cease to exist when the session expires, or may it remain in memory, inaccessible, until a later request takes the import lock?

quotes: The uploaded file is kept in the owner session that uploaded it, in the process's memory only — never in the store, never on a disk — until the import is accepted, another file is uploaded in that session, or the session ends (M11); then it is dropped.
Everything in it ends with the session.

An uploaded file is changed only by a holder of the import lock: an accepted import, holding it, drops every session's upload; the upload of a session ended by its limits is dropped by the next holder.
judgement.why: The model and first import rule say the upload is dropped when the session ends, while the later import rule retains it until a future import-lock holder drops it.

topics.topic: Backup discovery, naming grammar, prefixes, and filesystem namespace boundaries
questions: What exact prefixes, timestamp precision and encoding, filename grammar, directory depth and definition of a file being 'under' a prefix govern discovery, collision handling and deletion?
Exactly which filesystem entries may Registry inspect, remove, rename, or delete in the backup location?

quotes: First, it removes every file under the temporary prefix; if a removal fails, the run stops there.
Third, whatever the second step did, it deletes every kept backup made more than 30 × 24 hours before, and every file under the kept prefix whose unencrypted record (rule 1) cannot be read.

Kept and temporary names begin with two different prefixes the release declares; Registry removes, renames and deletes in the backup location only files under them, and the location is Registry's alone (A17).
A kept name is made from the backup's instant and is never overwritten: a backup whose kept name exists, or whose rename fails, is deleted and the run fails.
judgement.divergence: One implementation treats only regular direct children with the declared filename prefixes as managed files; another traverses directories or follows filesystem links beneath a prefix and may inspect or delete additional entries. The owner notices different retention, failures, collisions, or deletion of filesystem objects.
judgement.why: The destructive boundary depends on the undefined meaning of a file being under a prefix, including directory depth and link handling.

topics.topic: Path and containment resolution with symlinks or nonexistent components
questions: How does startup handle a missing final store file, a broken symbolic link, a symbolic-link loop, or a path whose existing parent resolves but whose final component does not yet exist?
How are symlinks and containment resolved when the store file or a path component does not yet exist, and does containment compare the store file, its parent directory, or both?

quotes: The store and the backup location are different places, neither inside the other, compared by their absolute paths with every symbolic link resolved; a configuration where they are the same or one holds the other fails the start.

When the store's configured file does not exist and its directory does, Registry makes a new, empty store of the running release's version there at the start; otherwise the store must open for reading and writing and carry the store version of the running release, and a store of another version, or one that does not open, fails the start — bringing a store to a new version is a step of the release, not of the start.
judgement.divergence: One implementation resolves the existing parent and appends a nonexistent store filename before comparing containment; another requires the complete path to resolve and refuses it, with further implementations differing on broken links and loops. The owner notices whether Registry starts, creates a store, or reports a configuration failure.
judgement.why: The required containment check does not define how full symbolic-link resolution applies to a store file that is expressly allowed not to exist.

topics.topic: Validation of all-token versus token-free owner-only configuration
questions: How does the ordered presence check distinguish the valid no-token owner-only mode from an invalid partial set of service tokens?
How does the presence check distinguish the valid all-four-token mode and the valid no-token owner-only mode from an invalid partially configured mode?

judgement.why: This is the same presence-rule question already answered: exactly all four tokens or none are valid, while a partial set fails.

precedent.topic: Presence rules that select owner-only versus service-token configuration
quotes:
It holds exactly these items and no other: the store's
   location; the backup location and the backup key (A18); the owner
   credential; one service token for each service of A09 — PresuPro, Client
   Portal, Cabinet, Cabinet Kernel (R0-20, R0-23) — or, for an owner-only
   start, none of the four: Registry then serves the owner interface alone
   and refuses every service call (A18 rule 9).

A configuration with some service tokens but without Client Portal's
   stops the start and names the missing item; one with none of the four is
   an owner-only start.
precedent.why: The texts expressly permit none of the four tokens for owner-only mode and reject a partial token set.

topics.topic: Whether accepted imports must lock other sessions before clearing their uploads
questions: Must an accepted import also take each affected session's lock before deleting that session's uploaded-file state, or is the uploaded-file field deliberately governed solely by the import lock despite being part of M11?
May an accepted import change another session's uploaded-file state without taking that other session's lock, or must it lock every affected session as well as the import lock?

quotes: Uploads and every other request that reads or changes an uploaded file — showing the mapping or the import's confirmation step, confirming, a sign-out — take the instance's one import lock first, then their session's lock (A13), check the closure while holding them, and hold both until done.

An uploaded file is changed only by a holder of the import lock: an accepted import, holding it, drops every session's upload; the upload of a session ended by its limits is dropped by the next holder.
judgement.why: The text assigns changes to uploaded files to the single import lock and expressly authorizes an accepted import holding that lock to drop every session's upload.

topics.topic: Whether session validity must be rechecked after waiting for the import lock
questions: If a request passes the session check and then waits for the import lock until its session's idle or absolute limit has passed, does it remain admitted under A13, or must session validity be checked again after both locks are acquired?

If an upload-related request passes the session check, waits for the import lock, and sign-out acquires the locks and ends the session first, must the already-admitted request still complete, or must it be refused after the session has ended?

judgement.why: This repeats the previously answered question about an admitted request continuing after concurrent sign-out or session termination.

precedent.topic: Whether admitted upload or confirmation requests survive concurrent sign-out
quotes:
A sign-out is applied in turn with the session's other requests that
   change it: one admitted before it completes its change to the store, and
   leaves nothing in the ended session.
precedent.why: A request admitted before sign-out completes its store change even if it acquires the session lock later, while no state remains in the ended session.

topics.topic: Backup scheduling behavior after a forward clock jump
questions: If the clock jumps from before 03:00 on one UTC date to after 03:00 on a later date that this process never observed before 03:00, is a run made for the newly observed date?

topics.topic: Byte encoding used for secret length, equality, distinctness, and constant-time comparison
questions: How are environment strings and presented credentials converted to bytes for the 32-byte test, equality, distinctness and constant-time comparison, especially for non-ASCII values?

topics.topic: Cleanup of temporary backup files left by failed startup
questions: When and how must a later start remove a probe or other temporary backup file left by a failed start?

topics.topic: Collision behavior when a kept backup destination name already exists
questions: Which file is deleted when the destination kept name already exists?

topics.topic: Cross-release compatibility of backup prefixes and record formats
questions: Must every release use stable prefixes and read all earlier backup-record formats, or may a new release ignore backups made under an older prefix or format?

topics.topic: Digest algorithm and byte representation for uploaded import files
questions: Which digest algorithm and byte representation identify an uploaded import file?

topics.topic: Exact ordering of configuration validation checks and reported items
questions: What exact ordering is used for environment-variable names and for the items said to be listed by rule 1, whose concrete names and full item order are not stated?

topics.topic: Handling disagreement between readable backup metadata and authenticated contents
questions: Are the unencrypted instant, release, audit sequence and key digest authenticated by the encrypted payload, and what must happen when the readable record disagrees with authenticated contents?

topics.topic: Retention and selection of old backup keys after rotation
questions: How is every still-kept backup's former key retained and selected after a backup-key rotation?

topics.topic: Whether secret validation requires entropy or merely a minimum byte length
questions: Must service tokens and the backup key contain 32 bytes of generated entropy, or is any 32-byte value—including a predictable one—valid?

topics.topic: Whether the backup erasure-retention period is a guaranteed hard maximum
questions: Is 31 days a hard maximum, a maximum only under an explicit successful-run timing assumption, or merely an expected schedule?
